ASML Soars 10% in a Week as Chip Stocks Bounce and Musk's Terafab Eyes a Million Wafers ©NASA/Bill Ingalls via Canva
Key Takeaways

ASML stock is up 10% in the past week as chip stocks rebounded and Musk's Terafab reportedly set a target of 1 million wafers a month.

Applied Materials and TSMC gained even more, so most of ASML's jump came with the group.

Customers are paying ahead for ASML's machines, and analysts expect its EPS to roughly triple from 2025 to 2028.

At about 23x forward earnings, the stock looks like a buy ahead of its Jan. 27 report.

ASML Holding (ASML:NASDAQ) is up 10% in the past week. That makes up for the 8% it lost on Nov. 5, when investors worried that Democrats' midterm wins would slow data-center spending.

Applied Materials (AMAT:NASDAQ) gained 16% and Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM:NYSE) gained 13% over the same stretch, while the Nasdaq 100 rose 5%.

Terafab adds fuel to a chip rebound

Most of the gain came on Monday, Nov. 9. That day, Nikkei Asia reported that Terafab, the chip project of Tesla and SpaceX, had told equipment suppliers it's aiming for 1 million wafers a month by 2032. That would take a lot of EUV machines, and only ASML sells them. Of course, it's only a target: Terafab hasn't built its first fab yet.

Applied Materials sells to the same chipmakers. After Thursday's close, it reported record quarterly revenue of $10.4 billion, up 53%. It also guided to about $11.1 billion for the current quarter.

TIKR tracks 41 analysts on ASML Holding. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on ASML Holding, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See ASML Holding's Analyst Ratings

Customers are still paying to wait in line

Third-quarter sales rose 55% to a record €11.7 billion. In the results release, CEO Christophe Fouquet said supply as currently planned for 2027 and 2028 "will not fully meet the demand of our customers." Some customers want to order for 2029 and 2030, and they're paying ahead: noncurrent contract liabilities jumped from €3.6 billion to €9.3 billion in the quarter.

TSMC, the customer I'd watch, said in October it's planning cautiously for 2027.

Analysts expect ASML's normalized EPS to roughly triple, from €24.71 in 2025 to €76.65 in 2028:

ASML Holding (ASML): normalized EPS, actual and consensus estimates, € per share, fiscal 2024-2029 (TIKR)
Still cheap against its own history

Even after the bounce, ASML sits 25% below its June 30 high. It trades at about 23x forward earnings. That compares with 47x at the end of June and a five-year average of 33x:

ASML (ASML): forward (NTM) P/E, last 5 years (TIKR)

The main risk is a slowdown in data-center spending, since ASML's plans assume chipmakers keep buying through 2028. CFO Roger Dassen has also said the MATCH Act, a proposed US ban on DUV immersion sales to China, could come up after the midterms. China is about 20% of ASML's expected 2026 sales.

title: Never bought Nvidia stock? Its slide could still hit your 401(k).
detail:
Never bought Nvidia stock? Its slide could still hit your 401(k).
Aimee Picchi
Fri, November 13, 2026 at 1:32 PM PST 4 min read
NVDA
^GSPC
SPY
^NDX
^DJI
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Even if you never bought a single share of Nvidia, the embattled chipmaker's steep slide this week could still ding your retirement savings.

Nvidia is a component of the S&P 500 and many other indexes, including the Nasdaq 100 and Dow Jones Industrial Average, all popular with retirement savers through funds offered by millions of employer retirement plans. About 97% of retirement plans now offer index funds, up from 79% in 2006, according to March research from the Investment Company Institute and ISS Market Intelligence.

That means even if you haven't directly bought Nvidia stock, your 401(k) is likely exposed to the chipmaker through an index fund, such as the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust or Vanguard's S&P 500 ETF (which trade under the tickers SPY and VOO, respectively).

Overall, Nvidia represents about 6% of the S&P 500 index, making it the second-largest component after Apple, according to Yahoo Finance.

Nvidia's shares started falling on Monday amid revelations that cofounder Jensen Huang had an extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Huang resigned from his role as CEO on Thursday, causing a further drop in the stock.

Since Nov. 6, the company's value has declined by more than $550 billion — a decline of about 13% in one week. While that will certainly hurt investors who directly own Nvidia shares, it may also impact people with indirect investments through funds that hold the chipmaker.

Nvidia's woes underline the risks inherent in many big tech companies widely held by U.S. investors, Shiva Rajgopal, a Columbia Business School professor who studies corporate governance, told CBS News.

The "Magnificent Seven" tech stocks account for about one-third of the S&P 500. As with Nvidia, several of those companies are closely associated with CEOs whom investors see as central to their success, such as Elon Musk at Tesla, Rajgopal noted. And as Nvidia's selloff showed this week, trouble for a charismatic CEO can quickly spill over into the company's stock.

"They are amazing wealth creators for shareholders," Rajgopal said. "But hopefully, shareholders know what they are doing when they buy the stock of these companies, because the exact same structure also has a lot of fragility built into it."

A drag on the S&P 500

The AI industry's influence on Wall Street was evident this week, as turmoil at Nvidia triggered a broader slump in technology stocks. Yet more companies within the S&P 500 rose rather than fell this week, boosting the index by 2.9% for the week through Thursday's close. Excluding Nvidia, the index would have gained an estimated 3.8%.

Falling knife or discount?

NVIDIA (NVDA) is down about 29% over the past month. The stock gave back its pre-market bounce this morning, so the slump continues. Whether it's a unique opportunity depends on separating the business from the headlines.

NVIDIA (NVDA): $161.76 (-2.66%) as of Nov 13, 10:09 AM EST (Market Cap: ~$3.91T) || 52W range $148.80–$243.37 || Forward P/E 17.8x || Daily RSI 24.6 (oversold)

Why it's falling

Three forces are stacked on top of each other:

Sector rout: the Nasdaq 100 and chip stocks sold off in early November on AI-regulation fears. Nvidia fell less than AMD. Read more (Nov 6, 2026)

Spending worries: investors are questioning how durable customer capex is. The stock lost about $630B in a month without any negative Nvidia news. Read more (Nov 2, 2026)
